title: Bridge1400
subtitle: Connecting waterfront culture to urban density
tools: Revit, D5 Render, AutoCAD, Photoshop, Illustrator, Google Earth Studio
intro: Bridge1400 sits on the threshold between Seattle's mercantile downtown and its waterfront. Instead of smoothing over that break, the project makes it spatial: a tall void cuts through the podium as a civic canyon linking Alaskan Way to Western Avenue.

A grand stair works as both passage and pause, and a slow ramp climbs past planted terraces with filtered views of Elliott Bay. Above the four-level retail and lobby podium, a mass timber hotel tower frames the water to the northwest and the city to the southeast.
facts: Glulam and CLT tower on a concrete podium
Retail, hotel lobby, restaurants, pool, 9 guest-room levels

sections.heading: Site
sections.text: Between Pike Place Market and the waterfront promenade, the site takes its cues from both: vertical density to the east, openness and movement to the west.
images: Site context: downtown Seattle and Elliott Bay

sections.heading: Sketches
sections.text: Hand sketches in section, plan and elevation explored how the floor plates stack, shift and turn toward the water.

sections.heading: Waterfront to city
sections.text: The site sits between two cultures: the open, moving waterfront to the west and the dense commercial city to the east. The building steps up between them.

image: Concept section: from the waterfront up to downtown

cards.title: Waterfront culture
cards.text: Ferries, piers, seafood markets and public promenades give the waterfront a culture of openness and flow. The building's glass and timber echo its marine and industrial traditions.

cards.title: Urban density
cards.text: Downtown's verticality and program intensity shape the eastern edge: functions stack vertically, while back-of-house services and circulation stay discreet.

cards.title: Hotel spaces
cards.text: The tower is a retreat above the city with panoramic views of Elliott Bay. Its mass timber structure brings warmth and quiet to the rooms.

cards.title: Retail spaces
cards.text: At street level, transparent frontage, varied tenant spaces and several entries make the podium the building's public interface.

sections.heading: Form
sections.text: Eight moves take the block from a full zoning envelope to the final form.
steps: A full-site envelope at a uniform 13 stories uses the whole allowable zoning volume.
A major cut along Alaskan Way reduces bulk and leaves a long tower parallel to Western Avenue, opening daylight to neighbors.
A deeper cut at the lower southeast corner, facing Union Street, makes room for a second tower mass.
A smaller, sloped volume interlocks with the main tower, adding tension and a dual massing language.
A 4-level base holds retail and the hotel lobby. A tall void at the corner draws pedestrians in.
Cuts at the southeast corner for egress stairs and at the southwest edge for direct retail and restaurant access.
A mid-block cut brings light into the podium core, and a cut on the east face opens a retail entry toward Alaskan Way.
A gently sloped internal ramp links Level 4 and Level 5 as a promenade with waterfront views.

sections.heading: Mass timber
sections.text: The four-level podium is concrete. Above it, the hotel tower is built in mass timber: glulam columns and beams carry CLT floors, arranged around concrete cores. Exposed wood gives the guest rooms warmth and quiet, carries the project's biophilic approach, and echoes the timber and glass of the working waterfront. Timber also stores carbon instead of emitting it, which the design study estimates below.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: The design study sizes renewable energy and water systems for the building. Rooftop and facade PV cover part of the annual electricity use, and low-flow fixtures, greywater reuse and rainwater harvesting cut potable water demand.
stats: Solar electricity per year, of 1,400 MWh used

sections.note: Estimates from the design study: PV yield about 1,410 kWh per installed kW; rainfall 38 in per year. Water strategies overlap, so their savings are not added together. CLT stores about 0.9 t CO2 per m3 (WoodWorks, U.S. Forest Service); car equivalent uses EPA's 4.6 t CO2 per car per year.
calc: Solar output: 150 kW × 1,410 kWh per kW per year = 211,500 kWh ≈ 212 MWh. 212 ÷ 1,400 MWh = 15% of annual use.
Electricity bill: 1,400,000 kWh × $0.11 per kWh (middle of the 10 to 12¢ grid price) ≈ $154K per year. The study's $105K implies 7.5¢, below its own grid price, so the grid price is used here.
PV cost: 150,000 W × $1.00 per W = $150,000 before incentives. Simple payback: $150,000 ÷ $23,000 ≈ 6.5 years.
Water share: 740K ÷ 2.3M gal ≈ 32%, rounded to 33% in the study.
Low-flow fixtures: 30 to 50% of 2.3M gal = 690K to 1.15M gal. Greywater: 40 to 50% of 2.3M gal = 920K to 1.15M gal.
Water cost: the study's $8K saved on 740K gal implies about $10.80 per 1,000 gal, so the full 2.3M gal bill is about $25K per year.
Rainwater: 38 in of rain per year × 0.623 gal per ft² per inch × about 10,000 ft² of roof ≈ 236,740 gal.
CLT storage: 0.9 t CO2 per m³ ÷ 35.3 ft³ per m³ ≈ 25 kg per ft³. 33,000 t ÷ 0.0255 t per ft³ ≈ 1.3M ft³ of timber, about 173,000 ft² of floor at 7.5 ft³ per ft².
Timber vs concrete: 33,000 t stored ÷ 4,500 t emitted ≈ 7.3 times (745% in the study).
Cars: 33,000 t ÷ 4.6 t CO2 per car per year ≈ 7,200 cars.
Carbon value: $6.2M ÷ 33,000 t ≈ $188 per tonne, in line with EPA's social cost of carbon (about $190 per tonne).

title: Professional Work
subtitle: Facade design at Plan to Perfection, Bangladesh
tools: AutoCAD, SketchUp, 3ds Max, D5 Render, Lumion, Photoshop
intro: For four years at Plan to Perfection I led facade and envelope design on residential towers, private homes, commercial buildings and a healthcare high-rise, many of them for developer WECON. Across 20 projects, about 150,000 sq ft, 12 are built or under construction.
I also produced the firm's visualization and cinematic animations, and received the firm's Best Architect award for design excellence in 2024.

title: Solaris
subtitle: Fueled by daylight: the fatigue-free workplace
role: Project lead designer in a five-person studio firm
team: Anthony Browning (principal), Isaiah Corp (project manager), Paul Golke and Liam Mitchell (designers)
tools: Revit, Rhino, D5 Render, AutoCAD, Photoshop, Illustrator
intro: Solaris turns a South Lake Union parking lot at 701 9th Ave N into a daylight-driven office and retail building. Work-related fatigue is widespread among US office workers, so the design treats daylight as the main tool for a healthier workplace.

Two light cuts pull morning and north light deep into the floor plates. Common brick ties the building to the neighborhood's historic fabric, and a base of translucent Kalwall panels turns the retail level into a glowing lantern at night.
facts: Living Building Challenge: Place, Health + Happiness, Beauty

sections.heading: Context
sections.text: From maritime industry to today's tech and life-science district, South Lake Union's history shapes the building's material choice and its public ground floor.
images: Neighborhood history and Living Building Challenge petals

sections.heading: Form and materials
sections.text: The upper mass spans the full site while the base pulls in to meet the street. A light tunnel on the east and a void on the north bring daylight in, and the core rises to a rooftop bar.
images: Massing steps, material axonometric and stacked levels

sections.heading: Envelope detail
sections.text: Wall sections resolve the brick veneer with relieving angles and brick ties, rigid and batt insulation, the Kalwall base and a walkable pedestal roof.

title: Forestreat
subtitle: Relaxation and well-being through nature
role: Co-designer. Site plan, the central courtyard void and rainwater reservoir concept, and all D5 renders
team: Maxwell T. Kyle (co-designer), Emily Dutton (interior designer)
tools: Revit, D5 Render, AutoCAD, Photoshop, Illustrator
intro: Forestreat draws on shinrin-yoku, the Japanese practice of forest bathing, to design an integrated primary care and behavioral health clinic. Trees soothe and restore, and here they also help remove the stigma of the healthcare setting.
A circular plan wraps a central courtyard. Radial services create gathering points for patients and community, and a canopy collects rainwater and channels it through a void to a reservoir below.
facts: Primary care, behavioral health, community spaces

sections.heading: Concept
sections.text: Leaves, branches, trunk and roots become a framework for the building's goals: well-being, equitable community, resources, change and integration.

sections.heading: Form
sections.text: A south-facing bar for daylight is curved into an organic form, opened by a central courtyard and an inviting void at the entry, then shaded by the rain-collecting canopy.

title: The Bussin Blocks
subtitle: Connecting city and neighborhood through a loop walk
role: Co-designer. Shared project concept and block-by-block design; form generation diagrams, AIA COTE Top Ten diagram and all D5 renders
tools: Revit, Rhino, D5 Render, AutoCAD, SketchUp, Photoshop, Illustrator, Tally, C.Scale
intro: The Bussin Blocks redevelop a 19-acre brownfield, a former veneer mill, into Post Falls' first walkable downtown. Surrounding streets extend into the site and set a block size small enough for real porosity.

A walking loop ties four nodes together: the preserved mill silo, the Centennial Trail, the neighborhood edge and a city gateway. Housing, a transit center in the reused mill structure, a museum, a hotel and a seasonal ice rink line the route.

sections.heading: Concept
sections.text: Four nodes create the loop journey. Six steps take the site from reused structures and a continued street grid to courtyard blocks with heights tuned to orientation.

sections.heading: Sustainability
sections.text: The mixed-use apartments are tested against the AIA COTE Top Ten: PV-ready roofs, rainwater collection, heat recovery DOAS, VRF heat pumps and rooftop beehives.
